Here's something that surprises most people: an LLM never sees your words. It only ever sees numbers.

Before your prompt reaches the model, a tokenizer chops it into chunks called **tokens**, which can be whole words, pieces of words, or even punctuation. Each token is then swapped for an ID number from a fixed vocabulary (GPT-4's has about 100,000 entries).

[EX]Imagine a tokenizer splits "Unbelievable!" into three pieces: "Un", "believ", "able", plus "!". The model receives something like [4821, 9077, 562, 0], and those ID numbers are made up for illustration. Different tokenizers use different IDs.[/EX]

[KEY]The model works on numbered chunks of text, not on letters or whole words the way you read them.[/KEY]

[Q]
Why does an LLM convert your prompt into tokens and numbers first?
A) Because it looks each word up in a database of stored answers
B) Because the model can only do math on numbers, not raw text
C) Because it translates your words into another language first
ANS: B
[/Q]
replies.user: (opener)

replies.raw:
Right, B. Everything the model does is arithmetic on numbers, so your text has to become numbers before anything else can happen.

Now for the next idea: what do those numbers *mean*? Each token ID gets swapped for a long list of numbers called an **embedding**, and tokens with similar meanings end up with similar lists, like neighbors on a map of meaning.

But a word's meaning depends on its neighbors, and that's where **attention** comes in. Each word can look back at the words before it and adjust its meaning accordingly.

[EX]Take "We walked along the river and sat down on the bank." The word "river" comes before "bank", so attention pulls "bank" toward riverside meaning. In "I put cash in the bank", "cash" pulls it toward money instead. Same token, different meaning.[/EX]

[KEY]Attention lets each word adjust its meaning based on the words that came before it.[/KEY]

[Q]
In "I put cash in the bank", what makes the model treat "bank" as a money bank?
A) Attention to the earlier word "cash" shifts its meaning
B) The tokenizer gives "bank" a different ID each time
C) The model looks up "bank" in a dictionary of definitions
ANS: A
[/Q]
replies.user: I picked B) Because the model can only do math on numbers, not raw text

replies.raw:
Exactly, A. "Cash" comes before "bank", so attention can use it to settle which meaning applies.

Let's keep going, because all that machinery serves one job: **next-token prediction**. After processing your prompt, the model produces a probability for every token in its vocabulary, picks one, adds it to the text, and repeats. That's how a whole answer gets written, one token at a time.

It isn't looking up an answer like a search engine. It's asking, over and over, "given everything so far, what usually comes next?"

[EX]Take "The cat sat on the ___". Words like "mat" or "floor" would get most of the probability, so the model is confident. For "My favorite thing to do on weekends is ___", thousands of continuations fit, so the probability spreads thin and the model is much less sure.[/EX]

[KEY]When one continuation dominates, the model is confident in it; when many fit, its confidence is spread out.[/KEY]

[Q]
Which blank would an LLM predict with the MOST confidence in its top choice?
A) "I put cash in the ___"
B) "She opened the door and said ___"
C) "The best name for a pet is ___"
ANS: A
[/Q]

It plays one game, over and over: **next-token prediction**. Given all the tokens so far, it scores every token in its vocabulary (GPT-4's tokenizer has about 100,000 of them) by how likely each is to come next.

It picks one, adds it to the text, and repeats. That loop, one token at a time, is how a whole answer gets written.

[KEY]An LLM writes by repeatedly predicting a likely next token, not by looking up a stored answer.[/KEY]

[EX]Take "The cat sat on the ___". The model might rate "mat" and "floor" as very likely, "couch" as fairly likely, and "refrigerator" as very unlikely. It samples from those odds, so the same prompt can produce different words on different tries.[/EX]

Here's something surprising: Common Crawl, a free archive of over 300 billion web pages, is a major source of the text that chatbots learn from.

So where does an LLM's knowledge come from? It starts with **pre-training**: the model reads a gigantic pile of text (web pages, books, code) and practices predicting the next token, over and over.

It doesn't memorize pages like a filing cabinet. It compresses patterns from all that text into its numbers, which is why it can write about things it never saw word for word.

[KEY]Pre-training is where a model's raw knowledge comes from: pattern-learning on huge amounts of text, not memorizing or looking up documents.[/KEY]

[EX]Imagine a model whose training text was collected up to a certain date. Ask it about something that happened after that date, and its built-in knowledge simply has nothing there. That date is called the training cutoff.[/EX]

[Q]
What best describes what a model does with its training text?
A) It stores every page and looks the answer up later
B) It saves the text and searches it like a search engine
C) It copies a similar page word for word when asked
D) It compresses patterns from the text into its numbers
ANS: D
[/Q]
replies.user: (opener)

replies.raw:
Correct. The model keeps patterns, not pages, which is why it can write fluently about things it never saw word for word.

But a model that has only done pre-training is a strange creature. It's trained to continue text, so if you type a question, it might continue with *more questions*, as if your message were the start of a quiz.

That's where **fine-tuning** and **RLHF** (reinforcement learning from human feedback) come in. People compare different answers the model writes and say which one they prefer. The model is then nudged toward the kind of answers people rate higher.

[KEY]RLHF turns a text-continuer into a helpful assistant by training it on human preferences about which answers are better.[/KEY]

[EX]In OpenAI's InstructGPT study (2022), people preferred answers from a 1.3-billion-parameter model trained with RLHF over answers from the 175-billion-parameter GPT-3, a model more than 100 times larger.[/EX]

[Q]
What did the InstructGPT result show about RLHF?
A) Bigger models are always preferred, whatever their training
B) A much smaller model with RLHF could beat a far larger one
C) RLHF taught the model new facts about the world
D) RLHF made the model 100 times larger overnight
ANS: B
[/Q]
replies.user: I picked D) It compresses patterns from the text into its numbers

replies.raw:
Exactly. RLHF didn't make the model bigger or teach it new facts. It changed how the model *behaves*, and people preferred that behavior.

Now the third idea. What a model knows comes from its training data, but that data has an edge.

A model's built-in knowledge stops at its training cutoff. Many popular chatbots can also search the web, so they can talk about recent news. But that's a separate tool bolted on: the model's own knowledge still ends at the cutoff, and what it finds online can be wrong.

[KEY]A model's own knowledge ends at its training cutoff; web search can add fresh information, but it doesn't change what the model learned.[/KEY]

[EX]Imagine a chatbot with a cutoff in early 2024, asked about a product that launched in late 2024. With search off, it has no knowledge to draw on and may guess. With search on, it can find pages about the product, but it might pick up an unreliable one.[/EX]

[Q]
A chatbot with web search gives a confident answer about last week's news. What's the best way to think about it?
A) The model's own knowledge still stops at its cutoff
B) Search turned the model's cutoff date into today's date
C) The answer came from search, so it can't be wrong
D) The model's training now includes last week's news
ANS: A
[/Q]
replies.user: I picked B) A much smaller model with RLHF could beat a far larger one

Right. Search is a tool the model uses; it doesn't rewrite what the model learned, and the pages it finds can still be wrong.

That first stage is called pre-training. The model reads that text (plus books and code) and learns patterns: which words follow which, how facts tend to be phrased, how arguments are structured. It isn't memorizing pages; it's compressing patterns.

[KEY]A model's built-in knowledge is compressed patterns from its training text, and it stops at a cutoff date.[/KEY]

[EX]Imagine a model whose training text ends in March. If you ask about a game that was played in June, its built-in knowledge has nothing on it, so it may guess or say it doesn't know.[/EX]

Let's keep going. Pre-training alone produces a model that is very good at continuing text, but not at being a helpful assistant.

If you typed "What is the capital of France?" into a raw pre-trained model, it might continue with more quiz questions, because that's a common pattern in its training text. It has absorbed a lot, but nobody has taught it to answer you.

That's where **fine-tuning** and **RLHF** (reinforcement learning from human feedback) come in. In RLHF, people compare pairs of model answers and pick the one they prefer. Those preferences train a reward model, and the chatbot is then adjusted to produce the kind of answers people rated highly.

[KEY]Pre-training gives a model knowledge, while fine-tuning and RLHF shape how it behaves, steering it toward answers people prefer.[/KEY]

[EX]In OpenAI's InstructGPT study (2022), people preferred answers from a 1.3-billion-parameter model trained with RLHF over answers from the 175-billion-parameter GPT-3, a model more than 100 times larger.[/EX]

A) How helpful the answers were to people.
B) How recent the model's built-in knowledge was.
C) How many web pages the model had read.

[/Q]

Pre-training gives a model a lot of knowledge, but it doesn't make it a good assistant. A model that only predicts the next token will happily continue your question with more questions, like a web page would.

**Fine-tuning** fixes this by training the model further on a smaller, carefully chosen set of examples, such as questions paired with good answers. The model's general knowledge stays, but its behavior shifts toward being helpful.

[KEY]Pre-training builds the knowledge; fine-tuning shapes how the model uses it.[/KEY]

[EX]Imagine a model that has read the whole internet. If you type "What is the capital of France?", a raw pre-trained model might continue with "What is the capital of Spain? What is the capital of Italy?", because quiz lists look like that online. After fine-tuning on question-and-answer examples, it replies "Paris."[/EX]

[Q]

A) Steering a pre-trained model toward useful behavior
B) Updating the model with this morning's news
C) Teaching the model to read the whole internet

replies.raw:
Yes, fine-tuning steers the model; it doesn't add the internet or this morning's news.

Fine-tuning on examples has a limit, though: it's hard to write down a perfect answer for every possible question. **RLHF** (reinforcement learning from human feedback) gets around this by asking people to do something easier: compare answers instead of writing them.

Here's how it works. The model produces several answers to the same prompt, and people rank them from best to worst. Those rankings train a separate **reward model** that learns to predict which answers people prefer.

Then the main model is trained to produce answers that score well with the reward model.

[KEY]RLHF teaches a model what people prefer, which is why it's the step that made models feel like assistants.[/KEY]

[EX]Imagine a model gives two answers to "Explain photosynthesis." One is a rambling paragraph full of jargon, and the other is clear and organized. A person ranks the clear one higher, and after thousands of rankings like this, the model learns to favor answers in that style.[/EX]

This is the step behind the InstructGPT result I mentioned: RLHF made a much smaller model beat GPT-3 in people's eyes.

[Q]
What does a human do in RLHF?
A) Rewrite the model's training data by hand
B) Rank the model's answers to show which they prefer
C) Check each answer for factual accuracy before release
ANS: B
[/Q]
